title: 1  Native gates and connectivity
text:
1.1 Pauli rotations
A circuit as written in an SDK is not what runs on a device. The hardware implements a small set of native gates, each a calibrated control pulse, and only between the pairs of qubits that are physically coupled. This section builds the one identity we need to read native gate sets, and then looks at what connectivity costs.
Every Pauli string is Hermitian and squares to the identity, \(P^2 = I\), because each single-qubit factor does. This one property is all we need for the following identity.

title: 1  Native gates and connectivity
text:
Definition 1.1 (Pauli string) A Pauli string on \(n\) qubits is a tensor product \(P = P_1 \otimes P_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes P_n\) with each \(P_j \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}\). We often drop the tensor product signs and write, for example, \(ZZ\) or \(XIY\).



Proposition 1.1 (Pauli rotations) Let \(P\) be a Hermitian operator with \(P^2 = I\), for example a Pauli string. Then for all real \(\theta\) \[
e^{-i\theta P/2} = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\, I - i \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\, P .
\tag{1.1}\]


Proof. Expand the exponential as a power series. Since \(P^2 = I\), even powers give \(P^{2m} = I\) and odd powers give \(P^{2m+1} = P\), so \[
e^{-i\theta P/2}
= \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^m}{(2m)!}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2m} I
\;-\; i \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^m}{(2m+1)!}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2m+1} P ,
\] and the two series are those of \(\cos(\theta/2)\) and \(\sin(\theta/2)\).


Example 1.1 (Single- and two-qubit rotations) Applying Equation 1.1 with \(P = X\), \(Z\) and \(Z \otimes Z\) gives \[
R_X(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\frac{\theta}{2} & -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\
-i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
R_Z(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\theta/2} \end{pmatrix},
\tag{1.2}\] \[
R_{ZZ}(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Z\otimes Z/2}
= \operatorname{diag}\!\left(e^{-i\theta/2}, e^{i\theta/2}, e^{i\theta/2}, e^{-i\theta/2}\right).
\tag{1.3}\] \(R_{ZZ}\) applies a phase that depends only on the parity of the two bits. That is why it can be built from two CNOTs and a single \(R_Z\) (Figure 1.1): the first CNOT writes the parity \(a \oplus b\) into the second qubit, \(R_Z\) applies the phase, and the second CNOT undoes the first.







Figure 1.1: The decomposition \(R_{ZZ}(\theta) = \gate{CNOT}\,(I \otimes R_Z(\theta))\,\gate{CNOT}\), drawn with Qiskit.









NoteWhere this returns



Equation 1.1 comes back twice later in the course: in Trotter circuits, where \(e^{-iHt}\) is split into Pauli rotations, and in the parameter-shift rule for gradients.

title: 1  Native gates and connectivity
text:
1.2 Native gate sets
Table 1.1 lists the native gates of some current platforms. Gate names and details change with each hardware generation; the point is the pattern. Every platform offers a continuous family of single-qubit rotations and one or two entangling gates.

The IQM gate is a rotation about an axis in the \(xy\)-plane of the Bloch sphere, \[
\gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi) = \exp\!\left[-i\frac{\theta}{2}\left(\cos\varphi\, X + \sin\varphi\, Y\right)\right].
\tag{1.4}\] The operator in brackets squares to the identity, so Proposition 1.1 applies to it too.

1.2.1 Why \(R_Z\) is free
On superconducting devices, \(R_Z\) is usually a virtual Z gate: no pulse is applied at all. The reason is the conjugation identity \[
R_Z(\alpha)\, \gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi)\, R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi+\alpha),
\tag{1.5}\] which follows from \(R_Z(\alpha) X R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \cos\alpha\, X + \sin\alpha\, Y\). Using Equation 1.5, every \(R_Z\) can be moved later through the circuit, changing the phases \(\varphi\) of the drive pulses it passes. CZ commutes with \(R_Z\), so nothing else changes. At the end, an \(R_Z\) right before a measurement in the computational basis has no effect and can be dropped.

title: 1  Native gates and connectivity
text:
1.3 Connectivity
A native two-qubit gate is available only between qubits that are physically coupled. The coupling graph records which pairs these are. On a superconducting chip it is fixed by fabrication: a square lattice, IBM’s heavy-hex lattice, or IQM’s star layout around a central resonator. In a trapped-ion chain all pairs can interact, at the price of slower gates.
A two-qubit gate between qubits that are not neighbours needs SWAP gates to bring them together, and each SWAP costs three CNOTs (Figure 1.2).






Figure 1.2: SWAP as three CNOTs with alternating control.



In practice we do not insert SWAPs by hand: transpilation maps a circuit onto the native gates and coupling graph of a device. We return to its cost with the algorithms; for now, remember that connectivity turns into extra two-qubit gates, and two-qubit gates are the main source of error (Preskill 2018).

Exercise 1.1 (Cost of distance)  

Check Figure 1.2 on the four computational basis states.
On a line of \(n\) qubits, how many CNOTs does a CNOT between the two end qubits cost, if the layout need not be restored afterwards? And if it must?

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
coupling graph

Graph whose vertices are qubits and whose edges are the pairs on which a native two-qubit gate is available.

native gate

A gate the hardware implements directly with a calibrated control pulse. Every other gate must be compiled into native gates.

Pauli string

A tensor product of single-qubit Paulis, P = P_1 ⊗ … ⊗ P_n with each P_j ∈ {I, X, Y, Z}. Hermitian, and squares to the identity.

transpilation

Compilation of a circuit into the native gates and coupling graph of a device, including inserting SWAPs and simplifying.

virtual Z gate

An R_Z rotation implemented by shifting the phase of all later drive pulses instead of applying a pulse. It takes no time and adds no error.
